Infrastructure demand keeps pushing Dell's results to record levels this quarter.

SUMMARY

Dell Technologies(DELL-11.83%)reported record quarterly results, with management stating that the company has transformed into an infrastructure-led organization where the Infrastructure Solutions Group drives the majority of revenue and profit. The company indicated that its expansion into AI-optimized servers has fundamentally shifted its financial profile, as evidenced by a $132.3 billion backlog and a 17% operating margin in its infrastructure business. Management reported that internal modernization efforts and the deployment of agentic AI have reduced operating expenses to 7% of revenue, the lowest level in the company's 42-year history. Strategic focus remains on meeting global demand for high-density compute, liquid-cooled data center architectures, and sovereign AI projects while maintaining a disciplined capital allocation framework through expanded share repurchases.

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator:Good afternoon, and welcome to the Fiscal Year 2027 Third Quarter Financial Results Conference Call for Dell Technologies Inc. I'd like to inform all participants this call is being recorded at the request of Dell Technologies. This broadcast is a copyrighted property of Dell Technologies, Inc. Any rebroadcast of this information in whole or part without prior written permission of Dell Technologies is prohibited.[Operator Instructions]I'd like to turn the call over to Paul Frantz, Head of Investor Relations. Mr. Frantz, you may begin.

Paul Frantz:Thanks, everyone, for joining us. With me today are Jeff Clarke, David Kennedy and Tyler Johnson. Our press release and presentation are on our IR website. The presentation includes additional content that complements today's discussion. During this call, we'll refer to non-GAAP financial measures unless we say otherwise. And you can find reconciliations to the most comparable GAAP measures in our press release and presentation. Growth rates are on a year-over-year basis, unless otherwise noted. We'll also make forward-looking statements based on our current expectations. These statements speak only as of today, and actual results could differ materially because of risks and uncertainties described in our presentation and SEC filings, including our most recent Form 10-K and Form 10-Q.

We assume no obligation to update them. Now I'll turn it over to Jeff.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke:Thanks, Paul, and thanks, everyone, for joining us. I am proud of how our team performed, delivering another record quarter with strong execution and growth across the business. Revenue was a record $54.9 billion, up 103%. Diluted earnings per share was a record $9.45, up 265%. We generated $4.5 billion of cash flow from operations and returned a record $4.9 billion to shareholders. Our proven operating model, competitive advantages, speed to market and ability to drive scale are all delivering compounding benefits. Our modernization efforts are driving significant operating leverage. Operating expenses were 7% of revenue, the lowest in our company's 42-year history.

ISG, our most profitable business, has grown significantly over the past several years and drives the vast majority of our growth and profit. In fiscal '24, the year we began selling AI servers, ISG generated 38% of our revenue. Over the last 4 quarters, that contribution has increased to 68%. The trend is even more pronounced within operating income, where ISG's contribution has gone from 54% to 83%, and I expect the trend to continue into our next fiscal year. Over the same period of time, ISG's operating income rate expanded 2 points.

We achieved that expansion despite the tremendous growth in AI servers, supported by strong growth in Dell IP storage, the insatiable demand for compute and the efficiencies generated by our modernization efforts. Technology is driving material business outcomes and the demand for AI infrastructure and data center modernization remains strong. As AI infrastructure becomes more complex, our competitive advantage strengthen and our momentum accelerates. Our engineering and design capabilities are differentiated. We develop purpose-built bespoke solutions optimized for each customer's specific requirements, often working through many design iterations that contemplate not just the infrastructure, but the data center as a whole, designed for power, cooling, efficiency and software.

Our technical teams are leveraging AI and the proprietary knowledge we've built over the last 13 quarters to streamline and accelerate the design work, allowing our engineers to deliver complex designs in hours and quickly work through a large number of iterations. Our procurement capabilities and world-class supply chain are differentiated, especially in today's constrained supply environment. In manufacturing, we fully test the complete solution at L11 and beyond, including full rack power up, thermal compliance and scale-out and scale-up network validation before anything ships. Our deployment services team can stand up a rack within 6 hours of delivery. Our on-site support services help customers achieve 99-plus percent utilization with fewer spares than our competitors.

Together, these capabilities get infrastructure live faster. On large deployments, we can deliver time to first token 4 to 6 weeks faster than competitors while providing industry-leading total cost of ownership. That allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably. And of course, innovation remains central to our advantage. In Q3, we were the first OEM to ship a fully liquid cooled networking rack, extending our first-to-market leadership. We are now the only OEM shipping DLC 100% scalable units across compute, accelerators and networking with a standard L11 rack design, and we will be shipping storage liquid-cooled L11 racks in the near future.

The proof point is in our order momentum, $180 billion over the past 4 quarters, with a majority of our new orders based on NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72. We also led the industry with the launch of our AMD-based PowerEdge R9815 and R9825 platforms, delivering 238 world records in industry benchmarks in the R9825 alone. At the same time, AI technology continues to advance rapidly. Models have progressed from one-shot responses to reasoning to recursive capabilities and now agentic systems that act, manage and orchestrate workloads. As customer zero, we are moving from using AI as a tool and an adviser to using AI as an operator.

The first wave of AI answered questions and delivering productivity improvements of 10% to 40%. In the use cases, we are seeing agents drive productivity improvements an order of magnitude better, 10x or more by accelerating work and putting intelligence directly in front of decision-makers. Realizing those outcomes starts with strong leadership. Companies must simplify, standardize, automate processes before digitizing them or augmenting them with intelligence. They must also modernize their data architectures, including semantic data layers that provide context around their data and intellectual property. Agents generate significant token demand, increasing the need for modern, disaggregated infrastructure across AI and traditional servers, Dell IP storage, data management solutions and networking.

While enterprise traction is accelerating, the vast majority of customers remain in proof-of-concept and tool adoption phase. The broader agentic adoption opportunity is still ahead of us. Overall, AI and the quest for intelligence is expanding our TAM across our portfolio. This is no longer simply about IT budgets. Data centers are becoming value centers, driving growth, productivity, speed and intelligence across the enterprise. Now let's start with the results. Starting with ISG. Revenue increased 198% to a record $42 billion. Operating income was $7.1 billion, with an operating income rate of 17%. In AI servers, demand continues to accelerate. In Q3, we booked $60.2 billion in AI orders and recognized a record $22 billion in AI server revenue.

We exited the quarter with a record $132.3 billion of AI server backlog. Behind every customer engagement and every order is a rigorous due diligence process, resulting in a fully vetted backlog. Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power. As I mentioned, each design is bespoke, optimized through multiple iterations with the customer. Through this tight collaboration, we know our customers well and have a high conviction that our backlog will convert to revenue. Our pipeline grew sequentially and remains multiples of our backlog, again, after converting $180 billion over the past 4 quarters. Additionally, our customer base and opportunity pipeline continues to diversify.

We now have over 7,500 Dell AI Factory customers. Our customer base spans neoclouds, sovereigns and enterprises. Within the neocloud segment, we remain highly selective about the partners we work with and the end customers supporting their demand. The global opportunity is expanding as more data centers are built outside of the United States. Across nearly every top country around the world, there are 2 to 3 sovereign projects. Enterprises were the fastest-growing portion of our opportunity pipeline expansion sequentially, providing further evidence that enterprise AI adoption is gaining traction. Internally, we continue to invest in our capabilities, ensuring we maintain our competitive advantage, deliver value for our customers and position for the substantial opportunity ahead. Moving to traditional servers.

Revenue was up 235% as demand remained exceptionally strong, supported by multiple growth drivers that are expanding our TAM. Enterprises increasingly recognize that compute is critical to both the growth and the operations of their business. They are buying more compute to accommodate growing workloads, refreshing their installed base and modernizing their data centers to free up power and space to be positioned for the AI era. Sequentially, we are seeing increased demand for CPU-based compute to support AI and inference workloads. Higher content continues to be a long-term secular tailwind. Servers contain more compute value with higher core counts, greater memory and storage capacity, increasing the value of each system.

Underneath all of this, cyber resilience and security are also driving refresh activity. Much of the installed base requires new hardware to meet current security and performance requirements. These needs cannot always be addressed through a software patch. We are executing very well in a supply-constrained environment, and we expect to gain share this quarter. Turning to storage. Revenue was up 24% as strong demand for our Dell IP portfolio drove revenue growth and improved profitability. Storage has always been critical as enterprise workloads and data grow. In the AI era, it is becoming even more important as data grows at exponential rates. Our storage opportunities are also expanding as AI evolves.

AI workloads are creating new demand drivers like key value caching, context layers and agents that need to store data, memory and state. For an enterprise, its data is its intellectual property, but siloed and without context, it's just data. Agents need that context, and that's why we've expanded the Dell AI Data Platform with a unified semantic layer and an enterprise knowledge graph. Together, they give nearly every application and agent the same trusted current view of the business without rebuilding context from scratch every query. This lowers token consumption, cuts compute costs and speeds time to production, all while keeping the customers' most sensitive data governed inside their own data center. Our storage offerings continue to expand.

Our Dell IP portfolio is resonating with customers, and we expect to gain share this quarter. Demand for Dell IP storage grew for the seventh consecutive quarter, and our Dell IP mix is at an all-time high. Demand remained broad-based with exceptional strength in North America. We also continue to see strong demand for unstructured storage, supporting AI workloads with triple-digit demand growth for the third consecutive quarter. PowerStore delivered a record demand and has now grown double digit or better for 10 consecutive quarters. PowerFlex grew double digits for 3 consecutive quarters and data protection delivered double-digit growth.

Storage growth, greater scale, the mix shift to Dell IP and meaningful sequential improvements in profitability at the solution level continue to be significant drivers for ISG profitability. Our Dell IP performance and accelerating pace of product development give us confidence in the opportunity ahead. Turning to CSG. Revenue grew 3% in a softer PC unit market as the industry adjusts to higher price points. Customers are prioritizing their budgets near term to servers and storage, electing to defer some PC-related refresh. The installed base continues to age, building deferred demand that we expect to refresh in the future. In closing, we continue to deliver a record year with record revenue, EPS, cash generation and capital return to shareholders.

The demand environment we see today remains strong and has not changed. Sophisticated customers are planning years in advance, giving us better visibility into future demand. AI server demand continues to accelerate, supported by a broadening customer base and expanding global opportunity. Our record $132.3 billion of AI server backlog has been fully vetted through our rigorous due diligence process. Traditional server demand remains strong, benefiting from traditional workload growth and aging installed base, heightened security requirements and the growing AI inference demand. Dell IP storage continues to grow and drive incremental profitability. As AI infrastructure becomes more complex, our competitive advantages are more pronounced and our TAM expands, increasing the need for modern disaggregated architecture.

Infrastructure demand continues to outpace supply. As we look into next year, the gap between component supply and end-user demand continues to widen. Our world-class supply chain is well positioned to navigate these constraints and deliver for our customers. Our operating model, speed to market growth and ability to drive scale are producing compounding benefits across the business. Together, these drive significant cash flow, shareholder return and long-term value for our shareholders. I'm proud of the team's performance and expect the momentum to carry into next year. With that, let me turn it over to David to walk through the financials and our outlook.

David Kennedy:Thanks, Jeff. The team executed exceptionally well, driving record revenue, record EPS and record shareholder returns. These results demonstrate the strength of our operating model, which is driving growth, expanding profitability and generating significant cash flow. Total revenue was up 103% to $54.9 billion. Gross margin dollars grew 105% to $11.7 billion. Gross margin rate was 21.2%, up 10 basis points. Operating expenses were up 20% to $3.8 billion, primarily due to variable compensation tied to our outperformance. We continue to drive significant operating leverage with OpEx down 480 basis points to 7% of revenue. Operating income grew 213% to $7.8 billion.

Operating income rate increased 490 basis points to 14.2% of revenue, driven primarily by scale and pricing discipline despite the impact of record AI mix. Net income was up 245% to $6.1 billion, primarily driven by strong operating income. Diluted EPS increased 265% to a record $9.45. Moving to ISG. ISG delivered record revenue of $42 billion, up 198%, marking the 11th consecutive quarter of double-digit or better revenue growth. AI server momentum continued to accelerate with $60.2 billion in orders, our second quarter with orders above $60 billion, a record $22 billion in revenue and $132.3 billion in ending backlog, all of which has been subject to our rigorous review process.

To expand on Jeff's comments, every customer goes through a credit oversight and due diligence process supported by DFS' risk management team. We evaluate the company, its financial capacity and its underlying end-user contracts. We run the due diligence process at 2 key points: when we agreed the purchase order and again before production begins, helping us actively manage risk. When we use DFS financing, it is selective and short term, bridging the customer from purchase order to cluster go-live. Traditional server and networking revenue was a record $15 billion, up 235%. Storage revenue was $4.9 billion, up 24%, with strong demand across our Dell IP portfolio, driving revenue growth and significant margin contribution.

Our margin-rich Dell IP storage demand has grown for 7 consecutive quarters, and our Dell IP mix is at a record high. ISG's Q3 operating income surpassed what we delivered in FY '26 and was a record $7.1 billion, up 308%, marking the 10th consecutive quarter of double-digit or better growth. Operating margin was 17%, up 460 basis points, primarily driven by scale. Building on last quarter, the benefits of scale continue to improve profitability across the entire portfolio. You're seeing that scale in the decoupling of revenue growth and operating expenses driven by 2 factors: strong demand is supporting record revenue. Additionally, our modernization efforts continue to drive operating expense efficiencies.

We also maintained strong operational and pricing discipline in a dynamic environment, reflecting the team's strong execution and continued focus on supporting our customers. Most of these benefits are structural and are reflected in our higher fourth quarter margin rate expectations. However, rates will sequentially moderate as the benefit from a stronger North America sales mix normalizes. Turning to CSG. CSG revenue was up 3% to $12.9 billion. CSG operating income was $0.7 billion or 5.5% of revenue, roughly in line with expectations. CSG provides important scale to our supply chain and drives significant cash generation given it's our most capital-efficient business. Moving to cash and the balance sheet.

We delivered another strong cash quarter with cash flow from operations of $4.5 billion, driven primarily by sequential revenue growth and higher profitability. We ended the quarter with $16.3 billion in cash and investments, up $2 billion sequentially, and our core leverage ratio is at 0.7x. We returned an all-time record $4.9 billion to shareholders this quarter, reflecting the second consecutive quarter of heightened shareholder return, averaging $4.6 billion against a $1.9 billion run rate last year. We repurchased 9 million shares at an average price of $488 per share and paid a dividend of approximately $0.63 per share.

Additionally, the Board of Directors approved a $25 billion increase in our share repurchase authorization, reflecting our confidence in continued strong free cash flow generation, commitment to shareholder return and long-term value creation. We remain committed to our long-term capital allocation framework, including our commitment to return at least 80% of adjusted free cash flow to shareholders. Turning to guidance. Given the momentum we are seeing in ISG, we're raising our fourth quarter revenue growth and non-GAAP diluted EPS expectations. We expect $56.25 billion revenue at the midpoint, up 69% year-on-year, driven by ISG growth of roughly 120%, with AI server revenue up sequentially to roughly $23.5 billion.

Traditional servers continue to grow triple digits with storage growing in the low teens. Operating expense is expected to remain roughly flat sequentially and just under 7% of revenue. We expect operating income rate to be roughly up 175 basis points with, both ISG and CSG similar year-over-year. We anticipate a diluted share count of roughly 634 million shares and I&O of roughly $450 million. Diluted non-GAAP EPS is expected to be $8.40 at the midpoint, up roughly 115% (sic) [ 116% ]. Our Q4 guidance implies a record FY '27 with record revenue of $202 billion, up nearly 80%.

Full year operating income rate is expected to be up roughly 350 basis points and is well above our expectations entering the year. Importantly, we expect this expansion despite the mix pressure of $78 billion in AI server revenue, more than 3x larger than last year. Non-GAAP diluted EPS is expected to be $29.68, up nearly 190% at the midpoint. And briefly on FY '28, as Jeff mentioned, demand in ISG remains robust and growth will be driven by multiple demand vectors. AI server demand continues to accelerate, and we will be well positioned to capture that growth. Data center modernization will drive growth in both traditional servers and storage.

Traditional workloads and data keep growing, aged installed bases need refreshing and customers are hardening cybersecurity. At the same time, inference and agentic workloads are extending infrastructure demand into traditional servers and storage. Within a supply-constrained environment, we continue to prioritize ISG. While we expect the PC unit environment to remain soft next year, the impact is manageable given the strength of our infrastructure business. While the base is much higher, the EPS levers we outlined at our Investor Day roughly a year ago remain the same. We continue to focus on revenue growth, margin accretion and operating leverage, which together drive significant cash generation and shareholder returns. In closing, we delivered another exceptional quarter with record year-to-date results.

Over the past 3 quarters, revenue was $145.8 billion, up 82%. Diluted EPS grew 231% to $21.32. We generated record cash flow from operations of $10.8 billion and returned an all-time record $11.2 billion to shareholders. The team executed exceptionally well with growth across the business. ISG demand remains robust. And in a supply-constrained environment, we continue to prioritize storage and servers. The modernization work we've been driving for the past several years helped drive operating expenses to 7% of revenue, an all-time low in our 42-year company history, while strengthening our competitive advantages across innovation, go-to-market, services and supply chain. We remain focused on capital efficiency and cash generation.

We're excited about Q4 and remain confident in our ability to create long-term value for our shareholders as we go into next year. Thank you to the team for their execution, and thank you all for your time today. Now I'll turn it back to Paul to begin Q&A.

Paul Frantz:Thanks, David. Let's go to Q&A.[Operator Instructions]

Operator:We'll take our first question from Mark Newman with Bernstein.

Mark Newman:Congrats on great numbers. Besides the strong revenue growth here, you've also got pretty strong operating margin improvement across all the ISG components. As we go forward, how do we think about how the operating margin will change going forward? Because I think you've got -- you've had this ability to benefit from rising costs of memory because you've had some supply constraints with your competitors, perhaps more supply constraints, you've passed on perhaps more than the cost increase. So not only is operating margin increased, but gross margin has also increased on a product-by-product basis. Just going forward, how should we think about that?

And what's embedded in this guidance regarding profitability for the main components of ISG, AI servers, traditional servers and storage?

David Kennedy:Sure, Mark. It's David here. I'll start. You're right. Look, the starting point here is the strong demand and ultimately the revenue growth in the ISG business. It's broad-based. So pick your geography, customer segment, customer vertical. It's as broad as it's ever been. It's obviously anchored with the $22 billion of AI shipments, which is a record and 35% higher than the previous record as we go even higher again in Q4. The traditional server growth, 235%, obviously drives the P&L. And look, ultimately, pleasing to see storage growth back up what we saw in Q2 and deliver 24% growth in Q3.

All that growth means from a rate perspective, the operating leverage that's driving into our P&L is exceptional. Our OpEx as a percentage of revenue within ISG improved 8 points year-on-year and 2 points quarter-on-quarter. So true scale and this idea of decoupling revenue growth from OpEx performance is truly on show and it validates our own modernization journey that we're doing within the company. And ultimately, that's sticky, that's structural and will endure as we kind of go forward from a P&L perspective. That OpEx obviously allows us then to absorb as we -- you see AI server grow almost 3x year-on-year. We're able to absorb that into the rate.

You saw ISG op inc up almost 5 points year-on-year to 17% of revenue. And ultimately, as we look into Q4, you're seeing more of the same. We've added revenue dollars. We've added margin dollars. We've added rate. So we've taken up the guide across the board in relation to that. And ultimately, that's what we'll look to do, continue to drive and see revenue growth totally decoupled from that, the OpEx performance. We'll continue to find scale, and we're committed to continued significant scale into the P&L, and it really sets us up well to drive growth going forward.

Operator:And we'll move to our next question from Amit Jawaharlaz Daryanani with Evercore.

Amit Jawaharlaz Daryanani:Jeff, you spoke about in your prepared comments about the gap between supply and demand continues to widen in reflection of what's going to happen next year, I think. And that's in a big stark contrast, I think, to what investors are worried about that AI spending might be approaching a peak fairly soon. Can you just unpack what do you think is driving the gap from your perspective in that supply-demand dynamic?

And then when I think about you folks getting to a Q4 revenue run rate of about $56 billion, without asking you for a formal fiscal '28 guide, can you just talk about which businesses or segments that you see have visibility to grow from this exit rate as you go into fiscal '28?

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke:Sure, Amit. I mean, look, as we have moved through the year, I think we've been consistently saying this demand is durable. The appetite or the demand for intelligence broadly continues. We've seen no slowdown of that. I think our AI orders of another $60 billion quarter. We now have $180 billion of orders in the last 4 quarters. We've shipped nearly $66 billion. All the while, the 5-quarter pipeline continues to build. We've added 4,500 Dell AI factory customers in the last 3 quarters. It was 3,000 in the first 8 quarters. It continues to grow. There are more customers in our 5-quarter pipeline than we have served to date.

All signs are pointing to the continued demand appetite for intelligence, particularly as we've moved from a training, which has driven the market initially to now inference making our way and progressing to agentic and ultimately to recursive learning. We see the pattern continuing. And in fact, we would say for the first 3 years of -- November '22 through October of '25, it was essentially a market driven by single shot sort of AI, you ask it a question, you get an answer. Now we're seeing that change where AI is becoming the doer or the operator. And we're seeing that same benefit inside of our own company.

David spoke to our record low operating expenditures and our modernization activities, all driven by the fact that we are seeing tremendous efficiency in our organization driven by now agentic. And we fundamentally look at this, you get asked why that's the case. It's real simple. Work is really 3 components. There's a component of work that you define what it is, you actually do it and you verify it. The action, the operating of the work is being increasingly moved towards agentic. And that is driving, we believe, an incredible growth rate in tokens and token consumption, the infrastructure that goes along with it, and we don't see that slowing down.

So when I look at the growth categories in our business and whether that's in our storage business, whether that's in our traditional server business and certainly on the AI side, it's inference, it's agentic. We're seeing KV cache need. We're seeing recursive learning need. We're seeing the agentic inference need, the resulting harnesses to operate this. And our forecast remain, I think, unchanged from the last time we talked about this topic. We still see tremendous token growth through the end of the decade. 87x, I think, was the last number I talked about, 3,600 quadrillion tokens. Training demand continues to grow 5x.

We're still tracking over 200 gigawatts of build-out of shells and power to provide the homes for all of this compute capability that is being needed. So again, no slowdown. I look at our own use inside our company. Our token growth is greater today than it was when the fiscal year began. Our use of agents, any given day, there are 100,000 agents spun up across our organization by our developers and knowledge workers consuming tokens. We have enterprise-wide agents driving a significant token use inside our company, driving again the efficiencies we talked about. And then we're going to double that number in the next 90 days.

So I think we as a kind of customer zero see this. The customers that we work with across neoclouds, across our sovereign and enterprise space continue to reinforce it. And we think the demand is very durable as reflected in our order rate and our backlog.

David Kennedy:And I think, Amit, I mean to build on that, and Jeff has set the table in terms of the robustness of the demand that we see, I think the linkage point tied to next year that you referenced. But if you think through our long-term value creation framework, and the tools of our toolbox in relation to EPS generation continue to be there, continue to be strong. So number one, growth that drives everything, with profitable growth back to the leverage of the OpEx and then ultimately generating free cash flow that we can return to our shareholders.

All of those give us a very agile list of tools in our toolbox that we can work with as we continue to observe the appetite for the intelligence in the ecosystem.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke:Yes. And maybe to wrap the bow and since you asked this portion of it, Amit, is -- and that demand is ahead of supply. In fact, we think the demand is further ahead of supply in calendar '27 than it's been in '26.

Operator:And we'll go to our next question from Ben Reitzes with Melius Research.

Benjamin (Ben) Alexander Reitzes:I wanted to talk about traditional servers a little bit. You obviously had a great quarter in there, but the guidance looks like it's down about 7% or 8% sequentially. And I was just thinking that maybe more CPU racks would slide in there by the fourth quarter. And I was wondering if you could just discuss how that's going to play out sequentially into calendar '27 when maybe we start to see the impact of agentic CPU racks and whether you're just being conservative with the fourth quarter with regard to that number going down sequentially?

David Kennedy:Yes. Thanks, Ben. Yes, look, as we look at our really pleasing performance in Q3, that 235% growth, looking to the Q4 guide, it's still a very impressive 137% growth guide that we've got in there. Ultimately, we're seeing this multiplicity of demand angles continue to come at us, whether it's the aged installed base and the growth in workloads in the traditional data center, the evolution of the AI and inferencing and obviously, cyber and security resiliency conversations continue to observe what we're looking at.

I think, look, from an operational perspective, we did touch on earlier this year our ability with the leverage and the ecosystem we have to transport some of our PC wafers into server supply for the back half of the year. We would have planned a lot of that for November. We probably got a little balance of that between October and November as we see that working through. But I guess we want to be clear, there's no change of course and speed in terms of the demand vectors that we're seeing from the traditional server space as we move forward.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke:Yes. Maybe some additional color, Ben, on the traditional server marketplace, $8.5 billion in Q1, $10.5 billion in Q2, $15 billion of revenue in Q3, $34 billion through the first 3 quarters. We did $19.5 billion last year, all of last year. So incredible results. The momentum is growing. And we see the vast majority of this demand coming from our existing customer base from small business to our largest enterprises that the demand is global in nature, North America in particular. We're seeing the continued -- what we've called out before is the modernization of data centers for power space and cooling.

David just mentioned the refreshing of the installed base, which has never been older at this time, and it's very significant. Our 17G products convert that at roughly a 7:1 ratio. Our 18G products convert that to a 12 to 14:1 ratio, so significant consolidation. And we see workloads inside the traditional enterprise growing, needing more compute. And then obviously, I think I mentioned in the prepared remarks, the notion of security and resiliency requirements driving demand. And the one you and I have talked about in the past is the fastest-growing area is the compute needed for the agentic AI and inference era running the harness.

And we're seeing this broadly across the neoclouds and enterprises, I think financial services, the EDAs and semi companies, HFTs, pharma, to name a few that are very advanced in their AI deployments. This is a 4-quarter trend. It is by far the fastest-growing part of our traditional server business. It initially started as inference. It's now agentic AI. I think as I mentioned just moments ago, that it will build towards recursive learning in the future. It's going to drive more demand. It continues to be a TAM expansion of the traditional server marketplace.

And in your modeling, I suspect we'll get to this, but to help everybody, the ASPs of agentic servers and inference servers are roughly twice the ASP of a traditional server. So we see significant growth. That demand continues to be out there. Getting supply, obviously, is key to fulfill it. And we're excited about the prospects of our traditional server business continuing to grow.

Operator:And we'll go next to Wamsi Mohan with Bank of America.

Wamsi Mohan:So you expressed a lot of confidence in converting the backlog and clearly, you guys have been doing a great job. But can you maybe just walk us through the potential impact in the event of data center delays, as you know, very well sitting in Texas, that has been a hot topic. And who bears the inventory and repricing risk if build-outs get delayed? And Jeff, maybe just to zoom out your perspective on if you expect any delays to be impactful in 2027 and 2028?

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke:Well, I think, Wamsi, the broader issue is we continue to track the orders and backlog. I think both David and I said in our prepared remarks that we have a vetting process. That vetting process is clearly the financial side of this. And ultimately, is there a building and is the building being complete and does it have the power and cooling capacity that it is, that it needs. We've been tracking that in this business since day 1. I think we've often said when asked about the gating items, this is a very complicated business, complex orchestration of many variables. We just talked about a couple of them. Is the site ready? Is power installed? Is cooling installed?

Can they receive the gear? Can we get the supply that's lined up with that, whether that be CPUs, whether that be memory, whether that be as silly things as optical transceivers and receivers? All of those play into the orchestration of being able to deliver to a customer. We've had no customers reschedule business. The backlog continues to be very firm. David can speak to the financial integrity of that backlog in just a moment. But we believe we have a high probability that, that backlog absolutely converts into shipments on the deliveries that we've committed to our customers. That backlog is over multiple quarters.

I won't get into segmenting it out by quarter, but the backlog is multi-quarter in nature. It's global in nature. It's across nearly 100 sites globally as many sites outside of the United States as inside the United States, distributed across many states within the United States. So we believe we're in a really good position when you look at where our customers are deploying gear. David?

We ended the quarter with $16.3 billion in cash and investments, up $2 billion sequentially, and our core leverage ratio is at 0.7x. We returned an all-time record $4.9 billion to shareholders this quarter, reflecting the second consecutive quarter of heightened shareholder return, averaging $4.6 billion against a $1.9 billion run rate last year. We repurchased 9 million shares at an average price of $488 per share and paid a dividend of approximately $0.63 per share.

Additionally, the Board of Directors approved a $25 billion increase in our share repurchase authorization, reflecting our confidence in continued strong free cash flow generation, commitment to shareholder return and long-term value creation. We remain committed to our long-term capital allocation framework, including our commitment to return at least 80% of adjusted free cash flow to shareholders. Turning to guidance. Given the momentum we are seeing in ISG, we're raising our fourth quarter revenue growth and non-GAAP diluted EPS expectations. We expect $56.25 billion revenue at the midpoint, up 69% year-on-year, driven by ISG growth of roughly 120%, with AI server revenue up sequentially to roughly $23.5 billion.

Traditional servers continue to grow triple digits with storage growing in the low teens. Operating expense is expected to remain roughly flat sequentially and just under 7% of revenue. We expect operating income rate to be roughly up 175 basis points with, both ISG and CSG similar year-over-year. We anticipate a diluted share count of roughly 634 million shares and I&O of roughly $450 million. Diluted non-GAAP EPS is expected to be $8.40 at the midpoint, up roughly 115% (sic) [ 116% ]. Our Q4 guidance implies a record FY '27 with record revenue of $202 billion, up nearly 80%.

Full year operating income rate is expected to be up roughly 350 basis points and is well above our expectations entering the year. Importantly, we expect this expansion despite the mix pressure of $78 billion in AI server revenue, more than 3x larger than last year. Non-GAAP diluted EPS is expected to be $29.68, up nearly 190% at the midpoint. And briefly on FY '28, as Jeff mentioned, demand in ISG remains robust and growth will be driven by multiple demand vectors. AI server demand continues to accelerate, and we will be well positioned to capture that growth. Data center modernization will drive growth in both traditional servers and storage.

Traditional workloads and data keep growing, aged installed bases need refreshing and customers are hardening cybersecurity. At the same time, inference and agentic workloads are extending infrastructure demand into traditional servers and storage. Within a supply-constrained environment, we continue to prioritize ISG. While we expect the PC unit environment to remain soft next year, the impact is manageable given the strength of our infrastructure business. While the base is much higher, the EPS levers we outlined at our Investor Day roughly a year ago remain the same. We continue to focus on revenue growth, margin accretion and operating leverage, which together drive significant cash generation and shareholder returns. In closing, we delivered another exceptional quarter with record year-to-date results.

Over the past 3 quarters, revenue was $145.8 billion, up 82%. Diluted EPS grew 231% to $21.32. We generated record cash flow from operations of $10.8 billion and returned an all-time record $11.2 billion to shareholders. The team executed exceptionally well with growth across the business. ISG demand remains robust. And in a supply-constrained environment, we continue to prioritize storage and servers. The modernization work we've been driving for the past several years helped drive operating expenses to 7% of revenue, an all-time low in our 42-year company history, while strengthening our competitive advantages across innovation, go-to-market, services and supply chain. We remain focused on capital efficiency and cash generation.

David just mentioned the refreshing of the installed base, which has never been older at this time, and it's very significant. Our 17G products convert that at roughly a 7:1 ratio. Our 18G products convert that to a 12 to 14:1 ratio, so significant consolidation. And we see workloads inside the traditional enterprise growing, needing more compute. And then obviously, I think I mentioned in the prepared remarks, the notion of security and resiliency requirements driving demand. And the one you and I have talked about in the past is the fastest-growing area is the compute needed for the agentic AI and inference era running the harness.

And we're seeing this broadly across the neoclouds and enterprises, I think financial services, the EDAs and semi companies, HFTs, pharma, to name a few that are very advanced in their AI deployments. This is a 4-quarter trend. It is by far the fastest-growing part of our traditional server business. It initially started as inference. It's now agentic AI. I think as I mentioned just moments ago, that it will build towards recursive learning in the future. It's going to drive more demand. It continues to be a TAM expansion of the traditional server marketplace.

And in your modeling, I suspect we'll get to this, but to help everybody, the ASPs of agentic servers and inference servers are roughly twice the ASP of a traditional server. So we see significant growth. That demand continues to be out there. Getting supply, obviously, is key to fulfill it. And we're excited about the prospects of our traditional server business continuing to grow.

Wamsi Mohan:So you expressed a lot of confidence in converting the backlog and clearly, you guys have been doing a great job. But can you maybe just walk us through the potential impact in the event of data center delays, as you know, very well sitting in Texas, that has been a hot topic. And who bears the inventory and repricing risk if build-outs get delayed? And Jeff, maybe just to zoom out your perspective on if you expect any delays to be impactful in 2027 and 2028?

That vetting process is clearly the financial side of this. And ultimately, is there a building and is the building being complete and does it have the power and cooling capacity that it is, that it needs. We've been tracking that in this business since day 1. I think we've often said when asked about the gating items, this is a very complicated business, complex orchestration of many variables. We just talked about a couple of them. Is the site ready? Is power installed? Is cooling installed?

Can they receive the gear? Can we get the supply that's lined up with that, whether that be CPUs, whether that be memory, whether that be as silly things as optical transceivers and receivers? All of those play into the orchestration of being able to deliver to a customer. We've had no customers reschedule business. The backlog continues to be very firm. David can speak to the financial integrity of that backlog in just a moment. But we believe we have a high probability that, that backlog absolutely converts into shipments on the deliveries that we've committed to our customers. That backlog is over multiple quarters.

And I think an example of that, if you look at our Q3 results, our financing receivables balance grew a modest $500 million quarter-on-quarter against the backdrop of shipping a record $22 billion of AI shipments. Operator:And we'll go next to Katherine Murphy with Goldman Sachs.

Katherine Murphy:Sticking on the traditional server business, can you help us think about both for the results in the quarter and embedded in outlook, the drivers across units versus pricing? And then you also noted expectations to gain share both on the traditional server and storage market. Can you talk about if you're seeing any better than historical attach on storage relative to history? Given the inflationary environment that we're operating in now, we don't think that's the correct way to measure the true value of what is happening in the server marketplace. There has been significant unit TAM destruction with the inflation that has been in the marketplace. If you take what has traditionally been 20% of the units, which have been 1P towers and 1P racks, that would have been 20-ish percent of the units, 2% of the revenue. That market under $3,000 servers is gone. So industry-wise, there are fewer units.

But what's interesting and I think very telling is the content of every server that we sold and shipped in the quarter was significantly different. Let me explain a little bit. So as we think about value and you think about these ratios that I mentioned earlier where an 18G server can consolidate 12 to 14 of our old 14G servers, that's built on a premise they're more capable. That capability is built on more cores, more DRAM and more NAND. We shipped and sold more cores in Q3 than we did the previous quarter and year-over-year.

We shipped more cores and more -- or excuse me, more bits of DRAM per server than we did last quarter and last year. And we shipped more bytes of storage in the servers we shipped this quarter than we did last quarter and last year. So the content per server is going up significantly, not inflation adjusted, absolute content, more cores, more bits, more DRAM per server, more productive, more powerful servers capable of being deployed, albeit in fewer units, taking on significantly greater workloads. That's what we're seeing in the marketplace. That has been, I think, consistent trend now for several quarters, and I think that will continue going forward.

On the storage side, a very -- it's a different trend, but a similar outcome. What we're seeing is greater attach of our higher-value storage products, our Dell IP portfolio. The Dell IP portfolio, we ran across a bunch of numbers, but 7 consecutive quarters of growth now. I think PowerStore has grown 10 consecutive quarters of double-digit growth. The unstructured products continue to grow quite nicely. The demand of them was in triple-digit range.

We are seeing more attach of storage in our AI business, particularly around the unstructured products, our PowerScale and ObjectScale product that continues to bode well as we go in the future because the demand drivers for storage in the future around the very same things that I described in servers, the agentic workload, agentic AI, KV cache, multimodal workflows and recursive learning all drive incremental storage. And in fact, incredible amounts of storage as you have to start looking at the traces and logs of every agent. If you start looking at the artifacts the agents create. If you look at some of the retrievable corpora that the agents create.

That is all driving significant storage growth and storage opportunities in the future. Again, it can go on with KV cache, the multimodal workflows when you start going into imaging, you start going to video, audio, sensor drives more bytes of storage that has to be ultimately stored. And ultimately, you're going to see that storage grows and grows and grows not by GPUs that are deployed, but by the bytes that have to be retained and that compound storage over time. Those are the growth drivers. That's where we're seeing the opportunities and where the focus of our business is.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke:Yes, Erik, I would step back maybe and look at it from an annual basis. From a macro view, when we look at the supply picture and our supply outlook, there's nothing that suggests that we're going to see price declines in enterprise NAND and DRAM for servers. The demand for those categories of memory continues to be way ahead of the supply. As more DRAM wafer capacity is set forth for GPUs and specifically building HBM, it comes at the expense of all other types of memory.

We think that crunch continues clearly into '27. And while the rate of inflation won't be the same as we saw in '26, we still believe the market is inflationary. Customers are spending their budgets today. We don't -- I don't know of a customer that's on the sideline that doesn't buy as much as they used to, but I'd also tell you that server they're buying today, if it's a 17G or an 18G server from us, is significantly more capable than the thing that it's replacing. So if you were to take a 14G that we sold 5 years ago, 4 years ago, and it's being retired, that product was $7,500, give or take.

While today's 18G product will be more expensive than that, it replaces 12 to 14 of them. The consolidation rate is significant and customers are benefiting from that. And while they're tying all of the questions together, while that may mean fewer units, it's a more capable machine, and that is what's being deployed in small businesses to the largest corporations in the world to meet their needs. But customers aren't on the sideline in servers. It would be different if we were talking about PCs. I think companies are deferring their PC purchases to ensure they have the infrastructure to work in what is going to be a very disruptive era with agentic technology really reinventing companies.

And that's what we see happening in the marketplace. So do I think the rate of increase slows? Yes. Do I still think that a significant price implication to our customers? Yes, because a smaller percentage on a large number is still a lot of dollars. Customers are spending their budgets. We see them active in the marketplace, and we believe that will continue into '27.

David Kennedy:And I think, Jeff, to build on that, I think the customers are trying to be resourceful and agile there, too, in terms of our DFS offering. So for investment-grade customers, the originations growth we've seen in PCs, storage and servers, up 55% in Q3. So you can see there's an appetite and the need to get infrastructure built out. So even in a budget crunch in the near term, the ability to turn CapEx into OpEx and understand what that looks like is a differentiated capability that we have in the marketplace. And I think our customers have appreciated the flexibility and being able to take advantage of that as part of their IT build-out.

Timothy (Tim) Long:I wanted to go back to the traditional server, some of the comments you made about a little bit more CPU type of servers to neoclouds and probably to sovereigns as well. Curious if you could just somehow quantify the pace or how that's looking, how margins look for those type of products? And then when you're selling these customers CPU servers compared to GPU servers, is the attach rate different? So maybe if you could just scale kind of how big and strong that business is and what it means for some of the other dynamics that we look at across the business?

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke:Sure. Let me try. A traditional server sold into a non-GPU application, and we separate the business, there's a GPU, that's the AI server business. There's the traditional server basis non-GPU based, which I tried to talk about earlier. The fastest-growing component of that is inference-driven and agentic AI-driven. It's not the largest portion of our traditional server business, which is our traditional enterprises and traditional applications, the things that we've talked about before. When I think about these servers going into these new workloads, it is across neoclouds who are deploying them that's in the financial services market.

It's in the EDA market, it's in the semis market, high-frequency traders, pharma, et cetera, they're very advanced in their AI deployments. They are driving agentic AI across their enterprises. And we believe that market continues to grow as the next iteration or evolution of agentic takes place, which is recursive learning. All of that drives more compute. More agents, more compute. The harness is essential to this. And the harness and the work that the harness does is really a CPU task. It's these things about how you manage containers, how do you manage sandboxes, manage I/O, how do you orchestrate that workload, which is CPU-driven is what we're talking about here.

And I referenced earlier, those types of servers are roughly twice the ASP as an enterprise-class server running an enterprise workload. The margins in those classes of devices as all of our -- across our server portfolio is well within our product-by-product internal marks that we make for our server products, and we feel very comfortable about that business and the prospects of growth are significant.

Paul Frantz:All right. And Jeff, please close it out.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke:Sure. Thanks, Paul, and thanks, everyone, for joining us today. All signs are pointing to the continued demand appetite for intelligence, particularly as we've moved from a training, which has driven the market initially to now inference making our way and progressing to agentic and ultimately to recursive learning.
